prompt: Dana's spouse died in 2023. Dana has not remarried, and her dependent son lived with her all of 2025 in a home she paid the full cost of keeping up. What is Dana's most favorable filing status for 2025?
choices: Married filing jointly
Single
Qualifying surviving spouse
Head of household
answer: Qualifying surviving spouse
explanation:
A taxpayer can use qualifying surviving spouse status for the two tax years after the year the spouse died. To qualify, the taxpayer must not have remarried, must have been able to file jointly in the year of death, and must pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home that is the main home, for the whole year, of a child, stepchild or adopted child the taxpayer can claim as a dependent.

Dana's spouse died in 2023, so the two following years are 2024 and 2025. She has not remarried and kept up the home all year for her dependent son, so she qualifies for 2025. This status uses the joint return tax rates and the joint standard deduction of $31,500, which is better than head of household ($23,625).

Exam tip: count the years carefully. Year of death is a joint return, the next two years can be qualifying surviving spouse, and after that the taxpayer usually moves to head of household or single.

source.title: Publication 501, Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information

prompt: What is the 2025 standard deduction for a single taxpayer who is under 65 and not blind?
explanation:
The 2025 law change increased the standard deduction for 2025. The basic amounts are $15,750 for single or married filing separately, $31,500 for married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse, and $23,625 for head of household.

A taxpayer who is 65 or older or blind adds an additional standard deduction on top of the basic amount: $2,000 for a single or head of household filer, and $1,600 for each qualifying condition for a married taxpayer. The question describes a single filer under 65 who is not blind, so only the basic $15,750 applies.

Exam tip: the exam tests the year shown in the question, here 2025. Watch for distractors that are last year's figure or the figure for a different filing status.

source.title: Publication 17, Your Federal Income Tax (2025)

prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the tests a person must meet to be a taxpayer's qualifying child?
choices: The support test
The relationship test
The residency test
The gross income test
answer: The gross income test
explanation:
There are two kinds of dependents. A qualifying child must pass five tests: relationship, age, residency, support (the child did not provide more than half of their own support) and joint return. A qualifying relative must pass a different set: not a qualifying child of anyone, member of household or relationship, gross income, and support (the taxpayer provided more than half).

The gross income test belongs only to the qualifying relative rules. A qualifying child can earn any amount and still be a qualifying child.

Exam tip: the two support tests point in different directions. For a qualifying child, ask whether the child supported themselves. For a qualifying relative, ask whether the taxpayer provided more than half the support.

source.title: Publication 501, Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information

prompt: Lars, a citizen of Norway with no green card, was physically present in the United States for 120 days in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025. Does he meet the substantial presence test for 2025?
choices: No. Counting all of 2025, one-third of 2024 and one-sixth of 2023 gives 180 days, which is fewer than 183
No. The test requires 183 days of presence in 2025 alone
Yes. Being present for at least 31 days in 2025 is enough
Yes. He was present for 360 days over the three years
answer: No. Counting all of 2025, one-third of 2024 and one-sixth of 2023 gives 180 days, which is fewer than 183
explanation:
A person who is not a green card holder is a U.S. resident for tax purposes in a year when they meet the substantial presence test. They must be present at least 31 days in the current year, and the weighted total must be at least 183 days. The weighted total counts every day in the current year, one-third of the days in the first year before, and one-sixth of the days in the second year before.

For Lars: 2025 counts 120 days, 2024 counts 120 ÷ 3 = 40 days, and 2023 counts 120 ÷ 6 = 20 days. The total is 180, three days short, so he is a nonresident alien for 2025 unless another rule applies.

Exam tip: write out the three lines of the calculation. Exam distractors often add the years at full weight or give the right answer with the wrong reason.

source.title: Publication 519, U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens

prompt: For 2025, Form 8615 (the "kiddie tax") can apply to a child whose unearned income is more than what amount?
explanation:
The kiddie tax stops parents from shifting investment income to children in lower brackets. It applies when a child has unearned income (interest, dividends, capital gains and similar income) above $2,700 for 2025, the child is under 18 at year end (or a student under 24 or an 18-year-old whose earned income doesn't cover half their support), a parent is alive, and the child doesn't file a joint return.

The first $1,350 of unearned income is covered by the child's standard deduction and the next $1,350 is taxed at the child's own rate. Unearned income above $2,700 is taxed at the parent's rate if it is higher, which is figured on Form 8615.

Exam tip: if the child's only income is interest and dividends under $13,500, the parents may be able to report it on their own return using Form 8814 instead.

source.title: Instructions for Form 8615, Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income

prompt: Which statement about the Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) is correct?
choices: It is filed electronically with FinCEN, separately from the tax return, when the combined value of foreign financial accounts was more than $10,000 at any time during the year
It is due June 30 and no extension is available
It is attached to Form 1040 and is required only if a single account held more than $50,000 on the last day of the year
It is required only for foreign accounts that earned taxable interest during the year
answer: It is filed electronically with FinCEN, separately from the tax return, when the combined value of foreign financial accounts was more than $10,000 at any time during the year
explanation:
A U.S. person (citizen, resident, or domestic entity) with a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file FinCEN Form 114 when the total of the highest values of all those accounts was more than $10,000 at any time during the calendar year.

The FBAR is filed electronically through FinCEN's BSA E-Filing System, not with the IRS and not with Form 1040. It is due April 15 and is automatically extended to October 15 with no request needed. Penalties for not filing can be large, especially for willful violations.

Exam tip: the aggregate rule means several small accounts can trigger the requirement. Two accounts with top balances of $6,000 each add up to $12,000, so an FBAR is required.

source.title: Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)
source.section: Who must file; When to file

prompt: A taxpayer files Form 4868 by the April due date of the return. What does the extension do?
choices: It removes the failure-to-pay penalty as long as the return is filed by October 15
It gives six more months to both file the return and pay the tax without interest
It gives four more months to file, and a second request adds two more
It gives six more months to file the return, but not more time to pay the tax
answer: It gives six more months to file the return, but not more time to pay the tax
explanation:
Form 4868 gives an automatic six-month extension of time to file Form 1040, moving the deadline for a calendar-year taxpayer from April 15 to October 15. No reason is needed, and filing it electronically or making a payment marked as an extension payment is enough.

The extension does not change when the tax is due. The taxpayer should estimate the tax and pay it by April 15. Interest is charged on any balance from April 15 until it is paid, and the 0.5% a month failure-to-pay penalty can apply unless at least 90% of the tax was paid by the original due date and the rest is paid with the return.

Exam tip: U.S. citizens living abroad get an automatic two-month extension to June 15 and can then use Form 4868 to reach October 15.

source.title: Publication 17, Your Federal Income Tax (2025)
source.section: Chapter 1: Extensions of Time To File

prompt: Priya, who is single, sold her main home in 2025 for a gain of $310,000. She owned and lived in it for the last six years and has never excluded a gain before. How much of the gain is taxable?
explanation:
Under section 121, a taxpayer can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of a main home, or up to $500,000 for most married couples filing jointly. The taxpayer must have owned the home and used it as a main home for at least two years during the five years before the sale, and must not have excluded gain on another home sale in the two years before.

Priya owned and lived in the home for six years, which satisfies both tests, and she has not used the exclusion before. Her taxable gain is $310,000 − $250,000 = $60,000, reported as a long-term capital gain on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

Exam tip: any part of the gain due to depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 (for example, for a home office) cannot be excluded, even when the total gain is under the limit.

source.title: Publication 523, Selling Your Home
source.section: Does Your Home Sale Qualify for the Exclusion of Gain?

prompt: After netting all of his 2025 sales, Omar, a single taxpayer, has a net capital loss of $11,000. How is the loss treated?
choices: The full $11,000 is deducted against other income in 2025
$3,000 is deducted against other income in 2025 and $8,000 is carried forward
Nothing is deducted in 2025 and $11,000 is carried forward for up to five years
$3,000 is deducted in 2025 and the rest is lost
answer: $3,000 is deducted against other income in 2025 and $8,000 is carried forward
explanation:
Capital gains and losses are netted first: short-term against short-term, long-term against long-term, and then the two results against each other. If the result is a net loss, an individual can deduct up to $3,000 of it against other income such as wages ($1,500 if married filing separately).

Omar deducts $3,000 in 2025. The remaining $11,000 − $3,000 = $8,000 carries forward to 2026, where it first offsets 2026 capital gains and then up to $3,000 of other income again. The carryover keeps its short-term or long-term character, and it continues until it is used up or the taxpayer dies.

Exam tip: corporations work differently. A corporation can only use capital losses against capital gains, carrying them back three years and forward five.

source.title: Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses
source.section: Limit on the deduction and carryover of losses

prompt: Mei received stock as a gift from her aunt. The aunt's adjusted basis was $4,000 and the stock was worth $9,000 on the date of the gift. No gift tax was paid. Mei later sold the stock for $12,000. What is her gain?
explanation:
Property received as a gift generally keeps the donor's adjusted basis (a carryover basis), increased by any gift tax paid on the appreciation. The special dual-basis rule applies only when the property's value at the time of the gift is less than the donor's basis, in which case the lower value is used to figure a loss.

Here the value at the gift ($9,000) was more than the aunt's basis ($4,000), so Mei's basis is $4,000. Her gain is $12,000 − $4,000 = $8,000. Her holding period also includes her aunt's holding period, so the gain is likely long term.

Exam tip: compare gifts with inheritances. A gift carries over the donor's basis, while inherited property generally gets a basis equal to its value at the date of death.

source.title: Publication 551, Basis of Assets

prompt: Ben inherited stock from his father. His father's basis was $20,000 and the stock was worth $50,000 on the date of death. No alternate valuation was elected. Ben sold the stock two months later for $53,000. What does he report?
choices: A $33,000 short-term capital gain
A $3,000 short-term capital gain
A $33,000 long-term capital gain
A $3,000 long-term capital gain
answer: A $3,000 long-term capital gain
explanation:
The basis of property acquired from a decedent is generally its fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the executor elects it on the estate tax return. This is often called a stepped-up basis, because any increase in value during the decedent's life is never taxed.

Ben's basis is $50,000, so his gain is $53,000 − $50,000 = $3,000. Even though he held the stock only two months, gain or loss on inherited property is automatically long term.

Exam tip: the step-up does not apply to income in respect of a decedent, such as a traditional IRA or unpaid wages. Those keep their character and are taxed to whoever receives them.

source.title: Publication 551, Basis of Assets

prompt: Which distribution from a traditional IRA taken before age 59½ is NOT subject to the 10% additional tax?
choices: A withdrawal used as a down payment on a vacation home
A withdrawal used to pay off credit card debt after a job loss
Up to $10,000 used to buy, build or rebuild a first home
A withdrawal used to buy a car needed to commute to work
answer: Up to $10,000 used to buy, build or rebuild a first home
explanation:
Distributions from a traditional IRA before age 59½ are generally subject to a 10% additional tax on the taxable amount, on top of regular income tax. The law lists specific exceptions, including death, disability, a series of substantially equal periodic payments, unreimbursed medical expenses over 7.5% of AGI, health insurance premiums while unemployed, qualified higher education expenses, a qualified birth or adoption (up to $5,000), and up to $10,000 for a qualified first-time home purchase.

A first-time homebuyer means someone who had no ownership interest in a main home during the two years before buying the new one. The $10,000 is a lifetime limit, and the money must be used within 120 days.

Exam tip: several exceptions apply to IRAs but not to 401(k)-type plans, and the reverse. Education and first-home exceptions are IRA-only, while the separation-from-service-at-55 exception is plan-only.

source.title: Publication 590b, Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs)

prompt: A credit card company canceled $20,000 of Rosa's personal debt in 2025. Immediately before the cancellation her liabilities were $12,000 more than the fair market value of her assets. No other exclusion applies. How much of the canceled debt is included in her income?
explanation:
Canceled debt is generally taxable income, and the lender usually reports it on Form 1099-C. One exclusion is insolvency: the taxpayer can exclude canceled debt up to the amount by which their total liabilities exceeded the fair market value of their total assets immediately before the cancellation.

Rosa was insolvent by $12,000, so she excludes $12,000 and includes the remaining $20,000 − $12,000 = $8,000 in income. She reports the exclusion on Form 982, and she must reduce certain tax attributes (such as loss carryovers or the basis of her property) by the amount excluded.

Exam tip: the insolvency worksheet counts all assets, including retirement accounts and pensions. Leaving them out can make a taxpayer look more insolvent than they are.

source.title: Publication 4681, Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments

prompt: What is the largest share of a taxpayer's Social Security benefits that can be included in taxable income?
explanation:
To figure how much of Social Security benefits is taxable, start with provisional income: modified AGI plus one-half of the benefits. If it is below the base amount ($25,000 for single, $32,000 for married filing jointly), none of the benefits are taxable.

Between the base amount and the second threshold ($34,000 single, $44,000 joint), up to 50% of benefits is taxable. Above the second threshold, up to 85% is taxable. The formula never includes more than 85%. A married person filing separately who lived with their spouse at any time during the year generally has a base amount of zero, so up to 85% is usually taxable.

Exam tip: these thresholds are not adjusted for inflation, so they are the same every year.

source.title: Publication 915, Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits

prompt: Kofi, age 40, had self-only coverage under a high deductible health plan for all of 2025. What is the most that can be contributed to his HSA for 2025?
explanation:
To contribute to a health savings account, a person must be covered by a high deductible health plan, have no other disqualifying health coverage, not be enrolled in Medicare, and not be claimable as someone else's dependent.

For 2025 the contribution limit is $4,300 for self-only coverage and $8,550 for family coverage. People 55 or older can add a $1,000 catch-up contribution. Kofi is 40 with self-only coverage for the whole year, so his limit is $4,300. This includes contributions from his employer. Contributions he makes himself are deductible on Form 8889 whether or not he itemizes.

Exam tip: under the last-month rule, someone who is eligible on December 1 can contribute the full year's amount, but must then stay eligible through the following year or part of the contribution becomes taxable.

source.title: Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans
source.section: Health Savings Accounts: Limit on Contributions

prompt: Tom's 2025 adjusted gross income is $60,000. He itemizes and paid $7,000 of unreimbursed qualifying medical expenses. How much can he deduct?
explanation:
Unreimbursed medical and dental expenses for the taxpayer, spouse and dependents are deductible as an itemized deduction only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of adjusted gross income.

Tom's floor is 7.5% × $60,000 = $4,500. His deduction is $7,000 − $4,500 = $2,500. Qualifying expenses include doctor and hospital fees, prescription drugs, insurance premiums paid with after-tax money, and certain long-term care premiums (subject to age-based limits). Over-the-counter drugs (other than insulin), cosmetic surgery and gym memberships don't count.

Exam tip: expenses reimbursed by insurance, or paid with tax-free HSA or FSA money, can't be deducted again.

source.title: Publication 502, Medical and Dental Expenses
source.section: How Much of the Expenses Can You Deduct?

prompt: A married couple filing jointly with modified AGI of $200,000 itemizes for 2025. They paid $18,000 of state income tax and $14,000 of real estate tax on their home. How much can they deduct for state and local taxes?
explanation:
For 2025 the total deduction for state and local income (or sales) taxes, real estate taxes and personal property taxes is limited to $40,000, or $20,000 for married filing separately. For taxpayers with modified AGI over $500,000 ($250,000 if married filing separately), the limit is reduced by 30% of the excess, but never below $10,000 ($5,000).

The couple paid $18,000 + $14,000 = $32,000. Their modified AGI of $200,000 is under $500,000, so the full $40,000 limit applies, and they deduct all $32,000.

Exam tip: taxpayers choose either state income tax or state sales tax, not both, and the choice counts toward the same overall limit. Foreign real property taxes are not deductible at all.

prompt: What must a taxpayer have to deduct a single cash contribution of $250 or more to a qualified charity?
choices: A qualified appraisal attached to the return
Form 8283 signed by an officer of the charity
Only a canceled check or bank statement showing the payment
A written acknowledgment from the charity, obtained by the time the return is filed, showing the amount and whether any goods or services were received in return
answer: A written acknowledgment from the charity, obtained by the time the return is filed, showing the amount and whether any goods or services were received in return
explanation:
Every cash contribution needs a record, such as a bank record or a receipt from the charity showing its name, the date and the amount. For any single contribution of $250 or more, the taxpayer also needs a contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the charity.

The acknowledgment must state the amount of cash, say whether the charity gave any goods or services in return, and describe and estimate their value if it did. It is contemporaneous if the taxpayer has it by the earlier of the date the return is filed or its due date including extensions. Without it, the deduction for that gift is disallowed entirely.

Exam tip: separate gifts are not added together for the $250 test. Ten separate $50 gifts don't need an acknowledgment, but one $500 gift does.

source.title: Publication 526, Charitable Contributions

prompt: For 2025, what is the maximum child tax credit for each qualifying child, and how much of it can be refunded as the additional child tax credit?
choices: $2,200 credit, all of which is refundable
$2,500 credit, of which up to $1,400 can be refundable
$2,200 credit, of which up to $1,700 can be refundable
$2,000 credit, of which up to $1,700 can be refundable
answer: $2,200 credit, of which up to $1,700 can be refundable
explanation:
For 2025 the child tax credit is up to $2,200 for each qualifying child who is under 17 at the end of the year and has a Social Security number valid for employment, issued by the return's due date. The credit phases out by $50 for each $1,000 of modified AGI over $400,000 for joint filers and $200,000 for everyone else.

If the credit is more than the tax owed, the taxpayer may get part of it refunded as the additional child tax credit, up to $1,700 per child. The refundable amount is generally 15% of earned income over $2,500. Dependents who don't qualify for the child tax credit, such as a 17-year-old or a parent, may qualify for the $500 credit for other dependents, which isn't refundable.

Exam tip: under the 2025 law, the taxpayer (or at least one spouse on a joint return) must also have a valid Social Security number to claim the credit.

source.title: Instructions for Schedule 8812 (Form 1040), Credits for Qualifying Children and Other Dependents

prompt: Which statement about the American opportunity tax credit is correct?
choices: It is worth up to $2,000 per return and none of it is refundable
It is available to students enrolled in a single course to improve job skills
It is worth up to $2,500 per eligible student, and 40% of it can be refundable
It can be claimed for any number of years of postsecondary education
answer: It is worth up to $2,500 per eligible student, and 40% of it can be refundable
explanation:
The American opportunity tax credit is 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified education expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000, for a maximum of $2,500 per eligible student. 40% of the credit, up to $1,000, is refundable.

The student must be pursuing a degree or other credential, be enrolled at least half time for at least one academic period during the year, not have finished the first four years of postsecondary education at the start of the year, not have claimed the credit for four earlier years, and have no felony drug conviction. Qualified expenses include tuition, required fees and course materials, but not room and board. The credit phases out between $80,000 and $90,000 of modified AGI ($160,000 to $180,000 joint).

Exam tip: the lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses per return (so $2,000 at most), is nonrefundable, and has no limit on the number of years.

source.title: Publication 970, Tax Benefits for Education

prompt: Each taxpayer below has earned income within the 2025 limits. Which one cannot claim the earned income credit?
choices: A taxpayer with $13,000 of investment income
A 30-year-old taxpayer with no qualifying child
A married couple filing jointly with two qualifying children
A head of household whose qualifying child has a valid Social Security number
answer: A taxpayer with $13,000 of investment income
explanation:
The earned income credit is a refundable credit for workers with low to moderate income. Besides the earned income and AGI limits, every claimant must have a valid Social Security number, must not file as married filing separately (with a limited exception for separated spouses), must be a U.S. citizen or resident alien all year, and must have investment income of no more than $11,950 for 2025.

Investment income includes taxable and tax-exempt interest, dividends, capital gain net income, net rental and royalty income, and passive income. The taxpayer with $13,000 is over the limit and gets no credit at all, however low their other income is.

Exam tip: the investment income test is a cliff, not a phase-out. One dollar over the limit removes the entire credit.

source.section: Rule 6: Your Investment Income Must Be $11,950 or Less

prompt: A working single parent paid $7,000 in 2025 for after-school care of her 9-year-old so she could work. What is the largest amount of expenses she can use to figure the child and dependent care credit?
explanation:
The child and dependent care credit applies to amounts paid for the care of a qualifying person so the taxpayer (and spouse, if married) can work or look for work. A qualifying person is a dependent child under 13, or a spouse or dependent who can't care for themselves.

For 2025 the expenses used to figure the credit are limited to $3,000 for one qualifying person and $6,000 for two or more, and also can't be more than the taxpayer's earned income. The credit is a percentage of those expenses, from 35% for AGI of $15,000 or less down to 20% for AGI over $43,000. This parent's credit is figured on $3,000, so it is between $600 and $1,050 depending on her AGI.

Exam tip: tax-free dependent care benefits from an employer reduce the $3,000 or $6,000 limit dollar for dollar.

source.title: Publication 503, Child and Dependent Care Expenses
source.section: How To Figure the Credit: Dollar Limit

prompt: Ruth is 67, single, has modified AGI of $60,000 and claims the standard deduction for 2025. Which statement about the new deduction for seniors is correct?
choices: It replaces the additional standard deduction for taxpayers 65 or older
It is available only on a joint return
She can deduct $6,000, in addition to her standard deduction and the existing additional standard deduction for age
She can claim it only if she itemizes deductions
answer: She can deduct $6,000, in addition to her standard deduction and the existing additional standard deduction for age
explanation:
For tax years 2025 through 2028, each taxpayer who is 65 or older by the end of the year can deduct an extra $6,000, or $12,000 when both spouses on a joint return qualify. The deduction is taken whether the taxpayer itemizes or claims the standard deduction. The qualifying person must have a valid Social Security number, and married taxpayers must file jointly.

The deduction is reduced by 6% of modified AGI over $75,000 ($150,000 joint). Ruth's $60,000 is under the threshold, so she gets the full $6,000. That is on top of her $15,750 standard deduction and the $2,000 additional standard deduction for being 65, for a total of $23,750.

Exam tip: the other new 2025 deductions (tips, overtime and car loan interest) are also available to non-itemizers, and each has its own income limits.

source.title: Working Families Tax Cuts: Tax deductions for working Americans and seniors

prompt: A self-employed person must file a return and pay self-employment tax when net earnings from self-employment are at least what amount?
choices: The amount of the standard deduction
explanation:
A taxpayer must file a return and pay self-employment tax if they have net earnings from self-employment of $400 or more, even if their total income is below the normal filing threshold. Net earnings are 92.35% of net profit from Schedule C or Schedule F, plus a partner's self-employment income from a partnership.

The $400 test applies to net earnings after expenses, not gross receipts. A freelancer who received $3,000 but had $2,800 of expenses has a $200 profit and no self-employment tax.

Exam tip: church employees who receive $108.28 or more in wages from an electing church or church-controlled organization also owe self-employment tax on those wages.

source.title: Topic no. 554, Self-employment tax

prompt: Which statement about self-employment tax is correct?
choices: One-half of the self-employment tax is deducted as an adjustment to income
All of the self-employment tax is deducted on Schedule A
It is figured on gross receipts before business expenses
It does not apply to a taxpayer who already receives Social Security benefits
answer: One-half of the self-employment tax is deducted as an adjustment to income
explanation:
Self-employment tax is the self-employed person's version of Social Security and Medicare taxes. The rate is 15.3%: 12.4% for Social Security on net earnings up to the 2025 wage base of $176,100 (reduced by any wages), and 2.9% for Medicare on all net earnings. It is figured on Schedule SE using 92.35% of net profit.

Because an employer can deduct its half of payroll taxes, a self-employed person deducts one-half of the self-employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1. This lowers AGI and income tax, but it doesn't reduce the self-employment tax itself.

Exam tip: for a $50,000 net profit, net earnings are $46,175, self-employment tax is about $7,065, and the adjustment is about $3,532.

source.title: Topic no. 554, Self-employment tax

prompt: The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to a married couple filing jointly when their combined wages and self-employment income are more than what amount?
explanation:
The Additional Medicare Tax is 0.9% of wages, compensation and self-employment income above a threshold based on filing status: $250,000 for married filing jointly, $125,000 for married filing separately, and $200,000 for all other filers. The thresholds are not indexed for inflation.

Employers must withhold the 0.9% once an employee's wages from that employer pass $200,000, regardless of filing status. Because a couple's threshold is based on their combined income, they may owe more or less than was withheld, and they settle the difference on Form 8959. There is no employer share of this tax.

Exam tip: don't confuse it with the 3.8% net investment income tax. That tax uses the same threshold amounts, but applies to investment income instead of wages.

source.title: Topic no. 560, Additional Medicare Tax

prompt: Li is single with modified AGI of $230,000, which includes $50,000 of net investment income. What is her net investment income tax?
explanation:
The net investment income tax is 3.8% of the smaller of two amounts: net investment income, or the amount by which modified AGI exceeds the threshold. The thresholds are $200,000 for single and head of household filers, $250,000 for married filing jointly, and $125,000 for married filing separately.

For Li, the MAGI excess is $230,000 − $200,000 = $30,000, and net investment income is $50,000. The smaller amount is $30,000, so the tax is 3.8% × $30,000 = $1,140, figured on Form 8960.

Exam tip: net investment income includes interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, royalties and passive business income. It excludes wages, self-employment income, IRA and pension distributions, and gain on a home sale that is excluded under section 121.

source.title: Net Investment Income Tax

prompt: Ken's 2024 adjusted gross income was $220,000. To avoid an underpayment penalty for 2025, his withholding and timely estimated payments must generally be at least the smaller of 90% of his 2025 tax or what share of his 2024 tax?
explanation:
A taxpayer generally avoids the underpayment of estimated tax penalty if they owe less than $1,000 after withholding and credits, or if their withholding and timely estimated payments are at least the smaller of 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax (provided last year's return covered 12 months).

For higher-income taxpayers, the prior-year safe harbor is 110% instead of 100% when the prior year's AGI was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately). Ken's 2024 AGI was $220,000, so he needs 110% of his 2024 tax, paid in four equal installments by April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.

Exam tip: withholding is treated as paid evenly through the year, whatever date it was actually withheld. Increasing withholding late in the year can therefore fix an underpayment from earlier quarters.

source.title: Publication 505, Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax

prompt: A family paid their nanny, who is their household employee, $9,000 in cash wages during 2025. How do they report the Social Security and Medicare taxes on those wages?
choices: On Schedule C, as a business expense
On Schedule H, filed with their Form 1040
On Schedule SE, as self-employment tax
On Form 1099-NEC, because no employment taxes apply
answer: On Schedule H, filed with their Form 1040
explanation:
A household employer who pays a household employee cash wages of $2,800 or more in 2025 must withhold the employee's Social Security and Medicare taxes (7.65%) and pay the matching employer share. A household employer who pays total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter also owes federal unemployment (FUTA) tax.

These taxes are reported on Schedule H and paid with the employer's Form 1040. Withholding or estimated payments can be increased to cover them and avoid an underpayment penalty. The family must also get an employer identification number, give the nanny a Form W-2 and file it with the Social Security Administration.

Exam tip: wages paid to the employer's spouse, to the employer's child under 21, to the employer's parent (in most cases), or to an employee under 18 who is a student aren't subject to Social Security and Medicare taxes.

source.title: Publication 926, Household Employer's Tax Guide
source.section: Social Security and Medicare Taxes; How Do You Make Tax Payments?

prompt: Ana worked for two unrelated employers in 2025. Each withheld Social Security tax correctly, but her combined wages were more than the $176,100 wage base. How does she recover the excess Social Security tax withheld?
choices: She cannot recover it, but it increases her future benefits
She files Form 843 with the Social Security Administration
She claims it as a credit against her income tax on her Form 1040
She asks each employer to refund its share
answer: She claims it as a credit against her income tax on her Form 1040
explanation:
For 2025 the Social Security tax is 6.2% of wages up to $176,100, so the most an employee should pay is $10,918.20. Each employer must withhold on wages it pays up to the wage base, without considering what other employers paid. An employee who works for two or more employers can therefore end up with too much withheld.

When the excess is caused by more than one employer, the employee claims it as a credit on Schedule 3 of Form 1040, which reduces the tax due or increases the refund. If a single employer withheld more than $10,918.20, the employee asks that employer to repay it, and files Form 843 only if the employer won't.

Exam tip: there is no wage base for Medicare tax, so excess Medicare withholding never happens this way.

source.title: Topic no. 608, Excess Social Security and RRTA tax withheld

prompt: A couple's joint refund was applied to the husband's past-due student loan, a debt from before the marriage. The wife had her own income and withholding. Which form does she file to get back her share of the refund?
choices: Form 8857, Request for Innocent Spouse Relief
Form 1040-X, Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return
Form 8379, Injured Spouse Allocation
Form 911, Request for Taxpayer Advocate Service Assistance
answer: Form 8379, Injured Spouse Allocation
explanation:
When a joint refund is offset to pay one spouse's past-due federal tax, state income tax, child support, spousal support or federal nontax debt (such as a student loan), the other spouse is an injured spouse if they are not legally responsible for the debt and made payments or had refundable credits that went into the refund.

The injured spouse files Form 8379 to have the refund allocated between the spouses, so their share is returned. It can be filed with the joint return, which prevents the offset in the first place, or by itself after the offset happens. It generally must be filed within three years of the return's due date or two years after the tax was paid.

Exam tip: remember the difference as "injured is about a refund, innocent is about a tax bill."

source.title: Reduced refund

prompt: In general, by when must a taxpayer file a claim for refund?
choices: Within two years after the return was filed or three years after the tax was paid, whichever is earlier
Within three years after the return was filed or two years after the tax was paid, whichever is later
At any time, as long as the original return was filed on time
Within one year after the IRS processed the return
answer: Within three years after the return was filed or two years after the tax was paid, whichever is later
explanation:
A taxpayer generally must file a claim for credit or refund (usually Form 1040-X for an individual) within three years from the date the original return was filed or within two years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later. A return filed before its due date is treated as filed on the due date.

The amount refundable is also limited by a lookback rule. A claim filed within three years can recover tax paid in the three years (plus any extension) before the claim. A claim filed under the two-year rule can recover only tax paid in the two years before the claim.

Exam tip: special longer periods apply to bad debts and worthless securities (seven years) and to foreign tax credits (ten years).

source.title: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund

prompt: Under a divorce decree signed in 2021, Jay pays his former spouse $2,000 a month in alimony. How are the 2025 payments treated?
choices: Jay cannot deduct them, and his former spouse does not include them in income
Jay cannot deduct them, but his former spouse includes them in income
Jay deducts them as an itemized deduction, and his former spouse does not include them in income
Jay deducts them as an adjustment to income, and his former spouse includes them in income
answer: Jay cannot deduct them, and his former spouse does not include them in income
explanation:
For a divorce or separation agreement executed after December 31, 2018, alimony and separate maintenance payments are not deductible by the payer and are not taxable to the recipient. Jay's decree was signed in 2021, so his payments have no tax effect for either of them.

Agreements executed before 2019 still follow the old rule: the payer deducts the alimony as an adjustment to income, and the recipient reports it as income. A pre-2019 agreement switches to the new rule only if it is modified after 2018 and the modification expressly says the new rule applies.

Exam tip: child support is never deductible or taxable under either rule, and a property settlement between spouses in a divorce generally isn't taxable either.

source.title: Publication 504, Divorced or Separated Individuals

prompt: A client asks about saving for a child's college costs in a section 529 plan. Which statement is correct?
choices: Distributions are tax free only if the beneficiary also claims an education credit for the same expenses
The account must be fully distributed by the time the beneficiary turns 18
Contributions are deductible on the federal return up to the annual gift tax exclusion
Earnings are not taxed when distributions are used for the beneficiary's qualified education expenses
answer: Earnings are not taxed when distributions are used for the beneficiary's qualified education expenses
explanation:
A section 529 qualified tuition program lets a family save for education. Contributions are made with after-tax money and aren't deductible on the federal return, but the earnings grow tax deferred. Distributions are completely tax free when they are used for the beneficiary's qualified education expenses: college tuition, fees, books, supplies, equipment, and room and board for students enrolled at least half time, as well as up to $10,000 a year of K–12 tuition.

If a distribution is more than the qualified expenses, the earnings part of the excess is taxable and is generally subject to a 10% additional tax. Contributions are gifts for gift tax purposes, and a donor can elect to spread a large contribution over five years of annual exclusions.

Exam tip: when coordinating with the American opportunity credit, set aside $4,000 of expenses for the credit and use the 529 distribution for the rest, so the same expenses aren't counted twice.

source.title: Publication 970, Tax Benefits for Education

prompt: A couple filed a joint return for 2023 and divorced in 2025. The IRS later assesses more tax on the 2023 return because of income the husband left off. From whom can the IRS collect?
choices: Each spouse, for half of the amount
Either spouse, for the full amount, unless the wife qualifies for relief
Only the husband, because the income was his
Only the spouse the divorce decree makes responsible for the tax
answer: Either spouse, for the full amount, unless the wife qualifies for relief
explanation:
When spouses file a joint return, each is jointly and individually (severally) liable for the entire tax, interest and penalties on that return. This remains true after a divorce, and even if the decree assigns the tax debt to one of them.

A spouse who didn't know about the error may be able to request relief on Form 8857. Innocent spouse relief applies when the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know of the understatement. Separation of liability relief divides the deficiency between divorced or separated spouses. Equitable relief covers other cases, including unpaid tax.

Exam tip: when advising on filing status, mention joint and several liability as a reason a spouse might choose married filing separately.

source.title: Publication 971, Innocent Spouse Relief

prompt: A married couple elects gift splitting for 2025. What is the most they can give to one child during the year without using any of their lifetime exclusion?
explanation:
The annual gift tax exclusion for 2025 is $19,000 per recipient. Gifts up to that amount to any number of people don't use any of the donor's lifetime exclusion and don't require a gift tax return.

With gift splitting, a married couple treats every gift either spouse makes to a third party during the year as made one-half by each. That lets them give $19,000 × 2 = $38,000 to the child, even if all of it comes from one spouse's money. Both spouses must consent, both must be U.S. citizens or residents, and the election applies to all gifts both of them make that year.

Exam tip: electing gift splitting requires filing Form 709, even when the split gifts are fully covered by the annual exclusions.

prompt: Which transfer is NOT a taxable gift, no matter how large it is?
choices: Forgiving a $50,000 loan to a brother
Adding a daughter as a joint owner of a rental property
Tuition paid directly to a university for a grandchild
A check given to a grandchild to cover tuition
answer: Tuition paid directly to a university for a grandchild
explanation:
Some transfers are excluded from gift tax without any dollar limit: tuition paid directly to an educational organization for someone, medical expenses paid directly to the provider for someone, gifts to a U.S. citizen spouse, gifts to qualifying charities, and gifts to political organizations.

The tuition exclusion covers tuition only, not books, supplies or room and board, and the payment must go straight to the school. A grandparent can pay $80,000 of tuition directly and still give the same grandchild $19,000 under the annual exclusion.

Exam tip: if a question says the donor gave the money to the student or parent, the unlimited exclusion doesn't apply, even if the money ends up paying tuition.

prompt: When is Form 706, the estate tax return, due?
choices: April 15 of the year after death
Nine months after the date of death
One year after an executor is appointed
Six months after the date of death
answer: Nine months after the date of death
explanation:
Form 706 is due nine months after the decedent's date of death, and any estate tax is due at the same time. The executor can request an automatic six-month extension of time to file on Form 4768. An extension of time to pay can be granted separately for reasonable cause.

A return is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts is more than the basic exclusion amount for the year of death: $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths ($15,000,000 for 2026). An executor may also file to elect portability even when no return is otherwise required.

Exam tip: keep the decedent's returns straight. The final Form 1040 is due April 15 of the year after death, Form 1041 is due on the estate's own schedule, and Form 706 is due nine months after death.

source.title: Instructions for Form 706, United States Estate (and Generation-Skipping Transfer) Tax Return

prompt: Al died in 2025 with an estate well under the filing threshold. His widow wants to be able to use his unused exclusion amount at her own death. What has to happen?
choices: Nothing. The unused exclusion passes to a surviving spouse automatically
The widow claims it on the couple's final joint Form 1040
Al's executor must file a complete Form 706 on time to elect portability
The widow files Form 709 within nine months of Al's death
answer: Al's executor must file a complete Form 706 on time to elect portability
explanation:
Portability lets a surviving spouse use the deceased spouse's unused exclusion (the DSUE amount) in addition to their own basic exclusion, both for lifetime gifts and at death. It is not automatic. The executor must elect it on a complete and properly prepared Form 706 filed on time, even if the estate is too small to otherwise require a return.

For estates that file only to elect portability, the IRS allows a simplified method that lets certain asset values be estimated, and Rev. Proc. 2022-32 allows a late election up to five years after the date of death in some cases.

Exam tip: the DSUE amount is fixed at the first spouse's death and is not indexed for inflation. If the survivor remarries, they can only use the DSUE amount from their most recent deceased spouse.

source.title: Instructions for Form 706, United States Estate (and Generation-Skipping Transfer) Tax Return

prompt: Which statement correctly compares Form 8938 with the FBAR?
choices: Both are filed with FinCEN and share the same $10,000 threshold
A taxpayer who files Form 8938 does not have to file the FBAR for the same accounts
Form 8938 is required only from taxpayers who live outside the United States
Form 8938 is attached to the income tax return, the FBAR is filed separately with FinCEN, and filing one does not replace the other
answer: Form 8938 is attached to the income tax return, the FBAR is filed separately with FinCEN, and filing one does not replace the other
explanation:
Form 8938 reports specified foreign financial assets and is attached to the income tax return. For an unmarried taxpayer living in the U.S., it is required when those assets are worth more than $50,000 on the last day of the year or more than $75,000 at any time during the year. Thresholds are doubled for joint filers and much higher for taxpayers living abroad. It covers foreign accounts and also foreign stocks, partnership interests and similar assets held outside an account.

The FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) is filed electronically with FinCEN, has a $10,000 aggregate threshold, and covers foreign financial accounts, including accounts where the person only has signature authority.

Exam tip: because the rules differ in who files, what is reported and the dollar thresholds, a taxpayer may have to file both, either one, or neither.

prompt: An individual forms a domestic LLC, is its only member, and files no entity classification election. How is the LLC treated for federal income tax?
choices: As a partnership filing Form 1065
As a C corporation filing Form 1120
As a disregarded entity, with its activity reported on the owner's return
As an S corporation filing Form 1120-S
answer: As a disregarded entity, with its activity reported on the owner's return
explanation:
Under the check-the-box rules, a domestic LLC's default classification depends on how many members it has. With one member, it is disregarded as separate from its owner. With two or more members, it is a partnership.

This LLC has one individual owner and made no election, so it is disregarded. The owner reports its income and expenses on Schedule C (or Schedule E or F, depending on the activity) and pays self-employment tax on the profit. The LLC is still treated as a separate entity for employment taxes and certain excise taxes, so it may need its own EIN if it has employees.

Exam tip: an LLC can elect corporate treatment on Form 8832, or S corporation treatment directly on Form 2553, which also counts as the election to be taxed as a corporation.

source.title: Limited liability company (LLC)

prompt: A married couple who file jointly are the only owners of an unincorporated business, and both materially participate. They elect to treat it as a qualified joint venture. How do they report the business?
choices: Each spouse files a separate Schedule C and Schedule SE for their share
They file Form 1120 and pay themselves wages
They file Form 1065 and give each other a Schedule K-1
One spouse reports everything on a single Schedule C
answer: Each spouse files a separate Schedule C and Schedule SE for their share
explanation:
A married couple who jointly own and operate an unincorporated business would normally have to file a partnership return. If they are the only members, both materially participate, and they file a joint return, they can elect to be a qualified joint venture instead.

Each spouse then reports their share of the income, deductions and credits (usually by ownership percentage) on their own Schedule C and pays self-employment tax on their own Schedule SE. Each spouse earns Social Security credit for their share, without the extra work of a partnership return.

Exam tip: a business owned through a state-law LLC generally can't elect qualified joint venture status, but in a community property state the spouses can choose to treat an LLC as a disregarded entity or as a partnership.

prompt: Which fact would prevent a domestic corporation from electing S corporation status?
choices: It has voting and nonvoting common stock with identical rights to distributions
One shareholder is a nonresident alien
One shareholder is the estate of a deceased shareholder
It has 75 shareholders
answer: One shareholder is a nonresident alien
explanation:
To elect S corporation status, a corporation must be a domestic corporation with no more than 100 shareholders (members of a family can be treated as one), have only eligible shareholders, and have only one class of stock. It must not be an ineligible corporation, such as certain banks and insurance companies.

Eligible shareholders are individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents, estates, and certain trusts and tax-exempt organizations. Partnerships, corporations and nonresident aliens can't be shareholders. A single nonresident alien shareholder makes the corporation ineligible, and if one acquires stock after the election, the election ends.

Exam tip: the one-class-of-stock test looks at rights to distributions and liquidation proceeds. Voting differences are allowed.

source.title: S corporations

prompt: A new calendar-year corporation wants its S election to take effect for its first tax year. By when must it file Form 2553?
choices: By the last day of that tax year
By the due date of its first income tax return, including extensions
Within 75 days after the end of that tax year
No more than two months and 15 days after the start of that tax year
answer: No more than two months and 15 days after the start of that tax year
explanation:
An S election is made on Form 2553, signed by all shareholders. To take effect for a given tax year, it must be filed at any time during the year before, or no more than two months and 15 days after the beginning of the year it is to take effect.

For a new corporation, the tax year begins on the earliest of when it has shareholders, acquires assets or begins doing business. For an existing calendar-year corporation, the deadline is March 15. An election filed after the deadline generally takes effect the following year.

Exam tip: a corporation that misses the deadline but had reasonable cause can often get relief under Rev. Proc. 2013-30 by filing Form 2553 within three years and 75 days of the intended effective date with the required statement.

source.title: Instructions for Form 2553, Election by a Small Business Corporation

prompt: When is Form 1065 due for a calendar-year partnership?
choices: April 15
January 31
March 15
May 15
answer: March 15
explanation:
A partnership must file Form 1065 by the 15th day of the third month after its tax year ends. For a calendar-year partnership that is March 15, the same as for an S corporation's Form 1120-S. Form 7004 gives an automatic six-month extension to September 15.

The March deadline exists so partners get their Schedules K-1 in time to file their own returns by April 15. Late filing carries a penalty for each month or part of a month (up to 12 months), multiplied by the number of partners: $245 per partner per month for returns due in 2025.

Exam tip: a weekend or legal holiday moves the deadline to the next business day.

source.title: Instructions for Form 1065, U.S. Return of Partnership Income

prompt: Nia joins a partnership by contributing $10,000 in cash and equipment with an adjusted basis of $25,000 and a fair market value of $40,000. The partnership has no liabilities. What is the basis of her partnership interest?
explanation:
Generally, no gain or loss is recognized when a partner contributes property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. The partner's starting basis is the money contributed plus the adjusted basis of the property contributed.

Nia's basis is $10,000 + $25,000 = $35,000. The partnership takes over her $25,000 basis in the equipment, and the $15,000 of built-in gain stays with her: if the partnership later sells the equipment, that gain is allocated to Nia.

Exam tip: liabilities change basis. When a contributing partner is relieved of debt, the relief is treated as a distribution of money that reduces basis, and gain results if it is more than basis.

source.title: Publication 541, Partnerships

prompt: A partnership pays one partner $30,000 a year for services, whatever the partnership earns. How is the payment treated?
choices: It is wages reported on Form W-2 with income tax withheld
The partnership deducts it, and the partner reports it as ordinary income subject to self-employment tax
The partnership cannot deduct it, and the partner reports it as a capital gain
It is a distribution that reduces the partner's basis and is not income
answer: The partnership deducts it, and the partner reports it as ordinary income subject to self-employment tax
explanation:
Guaranteed payments are payments to a partner for services or the use of capital that are figured without regard to partnership income. The partnership generally deducts them in figuring ordinary business income, unless they must be capitalized.

The partner includes the guaranteed payment in income for the partnership's tax year that ends with or within the partner's tax year. It is reported on Schedule K-1 and is subject to self-employment tax when paid for services. Partners aren't employees, so no income tax or FICA is withheld, and the partner generally pays estimated tax.

Exam tip: a partnership can report an ordinary loss after deducting guaranteed payments. The partner still includes the full guaranteed payment in income and then takes their share of the loss.

source.title: Publication 541, Partnerships

prompt: A partner's basis in his partnership interest is $15,000. The partnership distributes $22,000 in cash to him in a distribution that does not liquidate his interest. What is the result?
choices: He recognizes a $22,000 gain, and his basis is unchanged
He recognizes $7,000 of ordinary income, and his basis is unchanged
He recognizes no gain, and his basis becomes negative $7,000
He recognizes a $7,000 gain, and his basis drops to zero
answer: He recognizes a $7,000 gain, and his basis drops to zero
explanation:
A distribution is generally a tax-free return of the partner's basis. A partner recognizes gain only when money distributed (including a decrease in their share of partnership liabilities) is more than the adjusted basis of their partnership interest just before the distribution.

Here the partner receives $22,000 against a $15,000 basis. The first $15,000 reduces his basis to zero, and the remaining $22,000 − $15,000 = $7,000 is gain. The gain is treated as gain from selling a partnership interest, usually capital gain, though part can be ordinary if the partnership holds unrealized receivables or inventory items.

Exam tip: when figuring basis at year end, apply the year's income increases before distributions, and distributions before losses.

source.title: Publication 541, Partnerships
