prompt: A trust is required by its terms to distribute all of its income every year. What exemption amount does it deduct on Form 1041?
explanation:
Form 1041 allows a small exemption instead of a standard deduction. The amount depends on the type of entity: $600 for a decedent's estate, $300 for a trust required to distribute all its income currently (a simple trust), and $100 for all other trusts. A qualified disability trust can deduct a larger amount tied to the personal exemption.

The trust in the question must distribute all its income every year, so its exemption is $300. A simple trust also can't make charitable contributions or distribute principal during the year. If it does distribute principal, it is treated as a complex trust for that year and gets only the $100 exemption.

Exam tip: trusts and estates reach the top 37% bracket at only $15,650 of taxable income for 2025, which is why distributions to beneficiaries in lower brackets are often used to save tax.

source.title: Instructions for Form 1041 and Schedules A, B, G, J, and K-1

prompt: Which statement about the income tax return of a decedent's estate is correct?
choices: The estate can choose a fiscal year, as long as its first tax year ends within 12 months of the date of death
The estate files Form 1041 only if it distributes income to beneficiaries
The estate must use the calendar year, as most trusts do
The estate reports its income on the decedent's final Form 1040
answer: The estate can choose a fiscal year, as long as its first tax year ends within 12 months of the date of death
explanation:
A decedent's estate is a separate taxpayer from the date of death until the administration is finished. Its executor must file Form 1041 for any year in which the estate has gross income of $600 or more, or has a beneficiary who is a nonresident alien.

An estate can choose a calendar year or a fiscal year. Its first tax year can end on the last day of any month that is no more than 12 months after the date of death. Choosing a fiscal year can defer income for beneficiaries and make the timing of distributions easier to plan. Most trusts must use the calendar year, unless a section 645 election treats a revocable trust as part of the estate.

Exam tip: Form 1041 is due by the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), and Form 7004 extends it by five and a half months.

source.title: Instructions for Form 1041 and Schedules A, B, G, J, and K-1

prompt: A small tax-exempt charity normally has annual gross receipts of $30,000. What is the simplest annual filing that meets its requirement?
choices: No filing is required
Form 990-EZ
Form 990-T
Form 990-N, the e-Postcard
answer: Form 990-N, the e-Postcard
explanation:
Most organizations exempt under section 501(c) must file an annual information return or notice. The form depends on size. Organizations whose gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less can file Form 990-N, a short electronic notice. Organizations with gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000 can file Form 990-EZ. Larger organizations file the full Form 990, and private foundations always file Form 990-PF, whatever their size.

The charity normally has $30,000 of gross receipts, so the 990-N is enough. The returns are due by the 15th day of the fifth month after the organization's year end (May 15 for a calendar year).

Exam tip: churches, their integrated auxiliaries and conventions of churches don't have to file Form 990, 990-EZ or 990-N.

source.title: Annual exempt organization return: Who must file
source.section: Annual exempt organization return: Who must file

prompt: What happens when a tax-exempt organization fails to file a required annual return or notice for three years in a row?
choices: Nothing, as long as it had no unrelated business income
Its tax-exempt status is automatically revoked
It is put on probation and gets one more year to file
It pays a penalty of $100 a day until it files
answer: Its tax-exempt status is automatically revoked
explanation:
Under section 6033(j), an organization that is required to file Form 990, 990-EZ, 990-PF or 990-N and doesn't do so for three consecutive years automatically loses its tax-exempt status. The revocation takes effect on the original due date of the third missed return, and the IRS publishes the organization's name on its revocation list.

After revocation, the organization may owe income tax, and donors' contributions may no longer be deductible. To get exemption back, it must apply again on Form 1023 or 1024 and pay the user fee, even if it was never required to apply originally. Retroactive reinstatement is available in some cases if the organization shows reasonable cause or applies promptly.

Exam tip: small organizations that forget to file the 990-N e-Postcard are the most common victims of automatic revocation.

source.title: Automatic revocation of exemption

prompt: An exempt organization must file Form 990-T when its gross income from an unrelated trade or business is at least what amount?
explanation:
Unrelated business income is income from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and isn't substantially related to the organization's exempt purpose. An example is a museum running a full restaurant open to the public. An exempt organization with gross income from unrelated businesses of $1,000 or more must file Form 990-T, in addition to its regular annual return.

The tax is figured at corporate rates (21%) for organizations set up as corporations, or at trust rates for trusts. A $1,000 specific deduction is allowed. The organization must make estimated tax payments if it expects to owe $500 or more.

Exam tip: common exclusions from unrelated business income include work done by volunteers, sales of donated goods, dividends, interest, royalties and most rents from real property.

source.title: Publication 598, Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations

prompt: Which statement about a simplified employee pension (SEP) plan is correct?
choices: The employer must contribute the same percentage every year
Employees make salary deferrals of up to $23,500 for 2025
Only the employer contributes, up to the smaller of 25% of compensation or $70,000 for 2025
It must be set up by December 31 of the year for which contributions are made
answer: Only the employer contributes, up to the smaller of 25% of compensation or $70,000 for 2025
explanation:
A SEP lets an employer, including a self-employed person, contribute to traditional IRAs (SEP-IRAs) set up for each eligible employee. Only the employer contributes. For 2025, contributions for each employee can't be more than the smaller of 25% of compensation or $70,000, and compensation over $350,000 is ignored.

Contributions are discretionary from year to year, but in any year the employer contributes, it must use the same percentage of compensation for every eligible employee. Eligible employees are those who are at least 21, worked for the employer in at least three of the last five years, and received at least $750 in 2025. A self-employed person figures their own contribution on net earnings after the deduction for half of self-employment tax, which works out to about 20% of net profit.

Exam tip: a SEP can be set up and funded up to the due date of the business return, including extensions, so it is a useful planning tool after the year has ended.

source.title: Publication 560, Retirement Plans for Small Business

prompt: An employee under age 59½ takes a distribution from a SIMPLE IRA eight months after first participating in the employer's plan. No exception applies. What additional tax applies?
explanation:
Distributions from a SIMPLE IRA before age 59½ are generally subject to the 10% additional tax on early distributions, the same as other IRAs. If the distribution is made within the two years after the employee first took part in the employer's SIMPLE IRA plan, the additional tax rises to 25%.

The employee has participated for only eight months, so the 25% rate applies unless an exception (such as death or disability) is met. During those two years, money can be moved tax free only to another SIMPLE IRA. A rollover to a traditional IRA or employer plan is a taxable distribution.

Exam tip: a SIMPLE IRA plan is for employers with 100 or fewer employees who earned $5,000 or more, and the employer must contribute either a dollar-for-dollar match up to 3% of pay or a 2% nonelective contribution.

source.title: Publication 560, Retirement Plans for Small Business

prompt: At least two-thirds of a calendar-year farmer's gross income is from farming. How can she avoid an estimated tax penalty without making quarterly payments?
choices: Make one payment of 50% of the tax by June 15
File the return and pay all the tax due by March 1
Pay 90% of the tax in four equal installments
File the return and pay all the tax due by April 15
answer: File the return and pay all the tax due by March 1
explanation:
A taxpayer is a qualified farmer if at least two-thirds of their gross income in the current or prior year was from farming. Qualified farmers have special estimated tax rules. They can make a single estimated payment by January 15 of the following year, covering 66⅔% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax. Or they can skip estimated payments entirely by filing their return and paying all the tax due by March 1.

This farmer meets the two-thirds test, so filing and paying in full by March 1 avoids any underpayment penalty. If she files after March 1 without having made the January payment, a penalty can apply, figured on Form 2210-F.

Exam tip: gross income from farming includes Schedule F income, farm rental income from Form 4835, and gains from selling livestock, but not gains from selling farmland.

source.title: Publication 225, Farmer's Tax Guide

prompt: Hana actively participates in a rental house that lost $30,000 in 2025. Her modified AGI is $120,000, she has no other passive activities, and she is not a real estate professional. How much of the loss can she deduct this year?
explanation:
Rental activities are generally passive, and passive losses can only offset passive income. An exception lets an individual who actively participates in a rental real estate activity deduct up to $25,000 of losses against other income. Active participation is a low bar: owning at least 10% and making management decisions, such as approving tenants or setting rents.

The $25,000 is reduced by 50% of the amount modified AGI exceeds $100,000, and it is gone at $150,000. Hana's excess is $120,000 − $100,000 = $20,000. Half of that is $10,000, so her allowance is $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000. The other $15,000 of loss is suspended and carried forward until she has passive income or sells the property.

Exam tip: a real estate professional (more than half of personal services and more than 750 hours in real property businesses) who materially participates isn't limited by the passive rules at all.

source.title: Publication 925, Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules

prompt: Which group has unlimited rights to represent taxpayers before the IRS?
choices: Anyone who holds a preparer tax identification number (PTIN)
Enrolled agents only, because their license is federal
Annual Filing Season Program participants
Attorneys, certified public accountants and enrolled agents
answer: Attorneys, certified public accountants and enrolled agents
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.3 lists who may practice before the IRS. Attorneys and CPAs in good standing in any state, and enrolled agents, have unlimited representation rights. They can represent any taxpayer on any tax matter, at every level of the IRS (examination, collection and appeals).

Others have limited rights. Enrolled actuaries are limited to certain retirement plan matters. Enrolled retirement plan agents are limited to retirement plan issues. Annual Filing Season Program participants can represent only clients whose returns they prepared and signed, and only in limited settings. A PTIN alone gives no right to represent anyone.

Exam tip: enrolled agents earn their status from the federal government by passing the SEE or through qualifying IRS experience, so it applies in every state, while attorney and CPA rights come from state licenses.

source.title: Publication 947, Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney
source.section: Who Can Practice Before the IRS?

prompt: An unenrolled preparer holds a current Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion. Whom can the preparer represent, and where?
choices: No one. Only attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents can represent taxpayers
Clients whose returns the preparer prepared and signed, before any IRS office including Appeals and Collection
Clients whose returns the preparer prepared and signed, before revenue agents, customer service representatives and the Taxpayer Advocate Service
Any taxpayer, but only in examinations
answer: Clients whose returns the preparer prepared and signed, before revenue agents, customer service representatives and the Taxpayer Advocate Service
explanation:
The Annual Filing Season Program is a voluntary program for unenrolled preparers who complete continuing education each year, including a refresher course and test (some preparers are exempt from the test). A participant who has a Record of Completion has limited representation rights.

They can represent clients only for returns they prepared and signed, and only before revenue agents, customer service representatives and similar IRS employees, including the Taxpayer Advocate Service. They can't represent clients before Appeals officers, revenue officers (Collection), counsel or similar officers. The rights cover returns prepared and signed after December 31, 2015, while the preparer held a Record of Completion for both the year the return was prepared and the year of representation.

Exam tip: unenrolled preparers who aren't in the program have no representation rights for returns prepared after 2015.

source.title: Publication 947, Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney
source.section: Who Can Practice Before the IRS?: Unenrolled return preparers

prompt: A client wants her bookkeeper to be able to receive and inspect her confidential tax information, but not to act for her before the IRS. Which form does she sign?
choices: Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
Form 4506-T, Request for Transcript of Tax Return
Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
Form 56, Notice Concerning Fiduciary Relationship
answer: Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
explanation:
Form 8821 authorizes a person or organization (the designee) to inspect or receive the taxpayer's confidential tax information for the tax matters and periods listed. The designee doesn't need to be an attorney, CPA or enrolled agent, and can be anyone the taxpayer chooses.

Form 8821 does not authorize the designee to speak for the taxpayer, sign agreements, advocate for them, or receive refund checks. For that, the taxpayer uses Form 2848, and the representative must be eligible to practice before the IRS. Both forms are recorded on the IRS Centralized Authorization File.

Exam tip: the question's wording matters. "Receive or inspect information" points to Form 8821. "Represent," "advocate" or "negotiate" points to Form 2848.

source.title: Publication 947, Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney

prompt: Under Circular 230, which of these may a practitioner NOT do?
choices: Endorse or cash a refund check issued to a client
Charge a fee for preparing an amended return
Receive a client's refund check at the practitioner's office when the power of attorney authorizes it
Represent a client at an Appeals conference
answer: Endorse or cash a refund check issued to a client
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.31 says a practitioner who prepares returns may not endorse or otherwise negotiate (cash, deposit or transfer) any check, including a direct deposit, issued to a client by the government for a federal tax liability. A practitioner also may not direct or accept payment of a refund into the practitioner's own bank account or one they control.

The rule protects clients from losing control of their refunds. A practitioner can still receive the check on the client's behalf if Form 2848 authorizes it, as long as the check goes straight to the client.

Exam tip: a practitioner can't get around section 10.31 by having the client endorse the check over to the practitioner to pay fees. The client must handle the check and pay the fee separately.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: While preparing this year's return, an enrolled agent finds that the client left income off a return filed two years ago. What does Circular 230 require the agent to do?
choices: Withdraw from the engagement immediately
File an amended return for the client right away
Report the omission to the IRS within 30 days
Promptly tell the client about the omission and the consequences under the law
answer: Promptly tell the client about the omission and the consequences under the law
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.21 says a practitioner who is retained by a client on a matter before the IRS, and who knows the client hasn't complied with the revenue laws or has made an error in or omission from any return, must promptly advise the client of the noncompliance, error or omission and of the consequences under the law.

The practitioner's duty is to inform. Correcting the earlier return by filing an amended return is the client's decision. If the client refuses and the omission affects the current return (for example, through a carryover), the practitioner must consider whether they can still prepare that return under the standards of section 10.34, and may need to withdraw.

Exam tip: the answer to "what must the practitioner do?" under section 10.21 is almost always "advise the client," not "notify the IRS" or "amend the return."

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: A client fires her enrolled agent and asks for her records back, but she still owes the agent fees. In general, what must the agent do?
choices: Send the records to her new preparer but not to her
Promptly return the records she needs to meet her federal tax obligations, even though the fee is unpaid
Return the records only if the IRS issues a summons for them
Keep all the records until the fee is paid in full
answer: Promptly return the records she needs to meet her federal tax obligations, even though the fee is unpaid
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.28 requires a practitioner, at the client's request, to promptly return any and all records of the client that are necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations. The practitioner may keep copies. The existence of a fee dispute generally doesn't relieve the practitioner of this duty.

There is a narrow exception. If state law lets a practitioner keep records during a fee dispute, they need return only the records that must be attached to the client's return, and must give the client reasonable access to review and copy the rest.

Exam tip: "records of the client" include anything the client gave the practitioner and any return or document the practitioner prepared and gave to the client. Work papers the practitioner made for their own use are not client records, but a return prepared and not yet delivered because of unpaid fees may have to be handed over.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: A practitioner represents two clients despite a conflict of interest, after getting each client's informed consent in writing. How long must the practitioner keep the written consents?
choices: At least 36 months after the representation ends
At least 10 years after the representation ends
At least 12 months after the consents are signed
Until the next enrollment renewal
answer: At least 36 months after the representation ends
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.29 says a conflict of interest exists when representing one client is directly adverse to another client, or when there is a significant risk that the representation will be materially limited by responsibilities to another client, a former client, a third person, or the practitioner's own interest.

The practitioner may still represent a client if they reasonably believe they can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client, the representation isn't prohibited by law, and each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing at the time the conflict becomes known or within a reasonable period (no later than 30 days). Copies of the written consents must be kept for at least 36 months from the date the representation ends and be provided to the IRS on request.

Exam tip: 36 months also appears in section 10.30, for keeping copies of advertising and solicitations. Keep the 30-day and 36-month numbers straight.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: Under the text of Circular 230 section 10.27, for which service may a practitioner charge a contingent fee?
choices: Preparing an amended return to claim a larger refund, when no examination has begun
Representing a client in an IRS examination of an original return
Preparing an original income tax return
Giving advice on the tax treatment of a planned transaction
answer: Representing a client in an IRS examination of an original return
explanation:
A contingent fee is any fee based on whether a position is sustained, or that depends on the outcome, such as a percentage of the refund or tax saved. Section 10.27 as written generally bars contingent fees for services connected with matters before the IRS, with three exceptions.

The exceptions are: services in connection with the IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original return, or an amended return or claim for refund filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving written notice of the examination; a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties; and services in connection with a judicial proceeding. A practitioner may never charge an unconscionable fee.

Exam tip: a federal court (Ridgely v. Lew, 2014) held that the IRS can't enforce the contingent fee limits for preparing ordinary refund claims, but the exam generally tests the text of Circular 230.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: A practitioner publishes a written schedule of fees. For how long must the practitioner honor those fees?
choices: Until the end of the calendar year
No minimum applies
At least 10 business days
At least 30 calendar days after the last date the schedule was published
answer: At least 30 calendar days after the last date the schedule was published
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.30 lets practitioners advertise and publish fee information, such as fixed fees for specific services, hourly rates, the range of fees for particular services, and the fee for an initial consultation. A practitioner can't charge more than the published rates for at least 30 calendar days after the last date the fee information was published.

All advertising must be truthful and not misleading. An enrolled agent may describe themselves as "enrolled to represent taxpayers before the Internal Revenue Service" or "enrolled to practice before the IRS", but may not use the term "certified" or imply an employment relationship with the IRS. Copies of advertisements and a list of people sent direct-mail solicitations must be kept for at least 36 months.

Exam tip: uninvited in-person solicitation of tax shelter clients is banned, and practitioners may not use the IRS logo or suggest IRS endorsement.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: Which of the following is incompetence or disreputable conduct for which a practitioner can be sanctioned?
choices: Advising a client to take a position that has a reasonable basis and is disclosed
Declining to take on a new client during filing season
Charging hourly rates that are higher than other local practitioners charge
Willfully failing to file the practitioner's own federal income tax return
answer: Willfully failing to file the practitioner's own federal income tax return
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.51 lists conduct that can lead to censure, suspension, disbarment or a monetary penalty. It includes conviction of a crime under the federal tax laws or involving dishonesty, giving false or misleading information to the IRS, soliciting business by false statements, willfully failing to file one's own federal tax return or willfully evading tax, misappropriating client funds meant for the government, bribing or trying to influence IRS employees, practicing while suspended, and willfully disclosing tax return information without authorization.

Willfully failing to file one's own return is specifically listed. Practitioners are held to the same compliance standards as their clients, and the IRS checks practitioners' own filing during enrollment renewal.

Exam tip: "willfully" and "knowingly" are the key words in most section 10.51 items. Honest mistakes usually aren't disreputable conduct, though gross incompetence can be.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a sanction that can be imposed under Circular 230?
choices: Imprisonment
Suspension from practice
Censure
A monetary penalty
answer: Imprisonment
explanation:
Under Circular 230 section 10.50, the Secretary of the Treasury can censure, suspend or disbar a practitioner who is incompetent or disreputable, fails to comply with the regulations, or willfully and knowingly misleads or threatens a client. A monetary penalty can be imposed in addition to, or instead of, those sanctions, up to the gross income derived from the conduct. An employer or firm can also be penalized if it knew or should have known of the conduct.

These are administrative sanctions handled by the Office of Professional Responsibility, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing before an administrative law judge. Imprisonment comes only from criminal prosecution in court under the Internal Revenue Code, such as section 7206 for false returns.

Exam tip: censure is a public reprimand, suspension is for a set period of time, and disbarment is the most severe. A disbarred practitioner can generally petition for reinstatement after five years.

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service

prompt: What continuing education must an enrolled agent complete?
choices: 18 hours every year, including a 6-hour refresher course
40 hours every year, including 4 hours of ethics
72 hours every three years, with at least 16 hours each year including 2 hours of ethics
72 hours every three years, in any combination of years
answer: 72 hours every three years, with at least 16 hours each year including 2 hours of ethics
explanation:
Enrolled agents must complete 72 hours of continuing education during each three-year enrollment cycle. At least 16 hours must be completed each year, and 2 of them must be on ethics or professional conduct. Courses must come from IRS-approved continuing education providers, who report the hours to the IRS using the agent's PTIN.

Enrolled agents renew their enrollment every three years on Form 8554. The renewal cycle depends on the last digit of the agent's Social Security number. Someone newly enrolled partway through a cycle needs 2 hours for each month enrolled during that cycle, including 2 hours of ethics each year. Agents must keep records of completed CE for four years after the enrollment renewal.

Exam tip: the PTIN must also be renewed every year, separately from enrollment renewal. An enrolled agent who doesn't renew the PTIN becomes inactive.

source.title: Enrolled agents: Frequently asked questions

prompt: What is a CAF number?
choices: The number that identifies a firm as an authorized e-file provider
The control number the IRS assigns to an examination
A taxpayer's identity protection PIN
A unique nine-digit number the IRS assigns to a representative or designee who files a third-party authorization
answer: A unique nine-digit number the IRS assigns to a representative or designee who files a third-party authorization
explanation:
The Centralized Authorization File (CAF) is the IRS database of authorizations from Forms 2848 and 8821. The first time a representative or designee files one of these forms, the IRS assigns them a nine-digit CAF number. They enter it on every later authorization, which lets the IRS process the forms and send copies of notices to them.

The CAF number only identifies the person in the system. It doesn't show they are eligible to practice before the IRS. A representative without a CAF number can leave the box blank on their first form, and the IRS will assign one.

Exam tip: keep the identifiers straight. A PTIN identifies a paid preparer, an EFIN identifies an e-file provider, a CAF number identifies an authorized representative, and an IP PIN protects a taxpayer.

source.title: Instructions for Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative

prompt: How must the tax matters be described on Form 2848?
choices: By the notice number of the most recent IRS letter
By the type of tax, the tax form number and the specific years or periods
By the type of tax only, because the authorization covers every open year
By writing "all taxes, all years"
answer: By the type of tax, the tax form number and the specific years or periods
explanation:
Line 3 of Form 2848 must describe each matter by the type of tax (such as income, employment or excise), the tax form number (such as 1040 or 941), and the specific years or periods (such as 2023 and 2024, or the quarters ended March 31 and June 30, 2025). The IRS returns forms that use general references such as "all years" or "all taxes."

A power of attorney can list future periods, but only those ending no later than three years after the date the IRS receives the form. Civil penalties can be described as "civil penalties" with the years involved, and the form can't be used for matters unrelated to federal taxes.

Exam tip: a Form 2848 that doesn't meet the requirements, including a missing signature or date, is returned to the taxpayer and the representative isn't recorded on the CAF.

source.title: Instructions for Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative

prompt: A taxpayer files a new Form 2848 naming a new representative for the same tax matters and periods covered by an earlier one. What happens to the earlier power of attorney?
choices: It is revoked only if the new form is filed in the same year
It is revoked, unless the taxpayer checks the box to keep it and attaches a copy
It stays in effect, and both representatives are authorized
It stays in effect until the earlier representative withdraws in writing
answer: It is revoked, unless the taxpayer checks the box to keep it and attaches a copy
explanation:
Filing a new Form 2848 automatically revokes all earlier powers of attorney on file with the IRS for the same tax matters and periods. To keep an earlier power of attorney in effect, the taxpayer checks the box on line 6 and attaches a copy of each one to remain in effect.

A taxpayer can also revoke a power of attorney without naming a new representative by sending the IRS a copy of the earlier form with "REVOKE" written across the top, signed and dated. A representative can withdraw by sending a copy with "WITHDRAW" written across the top.

Exam tip: up to four representatives can be named on one Form 2848, and notices can be sent to up to two of them.

source.title: Instructions for Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
source.section: Line 6: Retention/Revocation of Prior Power(s) of Attorney

prompt: A taxpayer checks the "Third Party Designee" box on Form 1040 and names her preparer. What can the preparer do?
choices: Sign a consent to extend the statute of limitations for her
Talk with the IRS about the processing of that return, for up to one year after its due date
Represent her in an examination of that return
Receive her refund check
answer: Talk with the IRS about the processing of that return, for up to one year after its due date
explanation:
The third party designee checkbox on the return lets the taxpayer authorize a person, often the preparer, to discuss that return with the IRS. The designee can give the IRS information missing from the return, call about the status of the return, refund or payments, ask for copies of notices, and respond to certain IRS notices about math errors, offsets and return preparation.

The authorization covers only that return and automatically ends one year after the return's due date (without extensions), though the taxpayer or designee can end it earlier. The designee can't receive refund checks, bind the taxpayer to anything, or represent the taxpayer before the IRS.

Exam tip: for representation, use Form 2848. To receive information for other years or tax matters, use Form 8821.

source.title: Publication 947, Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney

prompt: The confidentiality privilege for communications between a taxpayer and a federally authorized tax practitioner covers which of the following?
choices: Advice given in a criminal tax investigation
Written advice promoting participation in a tax shelter
Communications made to prepare a tax return
Tax advice in a noncriminal tax matter before the IRS
answer: Tax advice in a noncriminal tax matter before the IRS
explanation:
Section 7525 gives communications between a taxpayer and a federally authorized tax practitioner (such as an enrolled agent or CPA) the same confidentiality protection that would apply to an attorney-client communication, but only for tax advice. Tax advice means advice given within the scope of practice before the IRS.

The privilege is limited. It applies only in noncriminal tax matters before the IRS and in noncriminal tax proceedings in federal court brought by or against the United States. It doesn't cover information gathered to prepare a return, communications in a criminal investigation, or written communications promoting a tax shelter.

Exam tip: if a civil examination turns into a criminal investigation, a non-attorney practitioner's privilege stops, so the client should consult a criminal tax attorney.

source.title: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund

prompt: A taxpayer filed her return on time but left off an amount that is more than 25% of the gross income shown on the return. There was no fraud. How long does the IRS have to assess more tax?
choices: Six years from the date the return was filed
Ten years from the date the return was filed
There is no time limit
Three years from the date the return was filed
answer: Six years from the date the return was filed
explanation:
The IRS generally has three years after a return is filed to assess additional tax, and a return filed early is treated as filed on its due date. The period is extended to six years if the taxpayer omitted from gross income an amount that is more than 25% of the gross income stated on the return. It is also six years for certain unreported foreign financial assets income over $5,000.

There is no time limit when a return is false or fraudulent with intent to evade tax, when there is a willful attempt to evade tax, or when no return is filed. The taxpayer and the IRS can agree to extend the period, usually on Form 872.

Exam tip: for the 25% test, gross income from a business means gross receipts before cost of goods sold, which makes the test harder to meet for businesses.

source.title: Time IRS can assess tax

prompt: In general, how long does the IRS have to collect a tax after it is assessed?
choices: 20 years
3 years
10 years
6 years
answer: 10 years
explanation:
Under section 6502, the IRS generally has 10 years from the date of assessment to collect a tax by levy or a court proceeding. The end of this period is called the collection statute expiration date (CSED). After it passes, the IRS generally can't collect the remaining balance, and any federal tax lien is released.

Certain events suspend (toll) the 10-year period. These include a pending offer in compromise, a pending installment agreement request, a timely collection due process hearing request, bankruptcy, the taxpayer living outside the U.S. for six months or more, and a request for innocent spouse relief.

Exam tip: each assessment has its own CSED, so an additional tax assessed after an audit starts a new 10-year period for that amount.

source.title: Time IRS can collect tax

prompt: A taxpayer living in the United States receives a notice of deficiency. How long does she have to petition the Tax Court?
choices: 150 days from the date of the notice
30 days from the date of the notice
90 days from the date of the notice
One year from the date of the notice
answer: 90 days from the date of the notice
explanation:
A notice of deficiency, often called the 90-day letter or statutory notice, is the IRS's formal notice of proposed additional tax. It gives the taxpayer 90 days from the date of mailing (150 days if addressed to a person outside the United States) to file a petition with the U.S. Tax Court. The notice states the last day to file.

Filing on time lets the taxpayer dispute the tax in Tax Court without paying it first, and the IRS can't assess the tax while the case is pending. If the deadline passes, the IRS assesses the tax. The taxpayer's remaining option is then usually to pay and sue for a refund in district court or the Court of Federal Claims.

Exam tip: the 30-day letter (which offers Appeals) comes first, and the 90-day letter comes after. The IRS can't extend the 90-day deadline.

source.title: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund
source.section: Appeals to the Courts: Tax Court

prompt: A taxpayer may ask the Tax Court to use its simplified small tax case procedure when the amount in dispute for each tax year is not more than what amount?
explanation:
The Tax Court's small tax case procedure (an "S case") is available when the amount in dispute, including penalties, is $50,000 or less for any one tax year or period. For collection due process cases, the limit is the total unpaid tax of $50,000 or less.

S cases are less formal. Taxpayers often represent themselves, the rules of evidence are relaxed, and trials are held in more cities. The tradeoff is that the decision is final and can't be appealed by either the taxpayer or the IRS, and it can't be used as precedent in other cases.

Exam tip: the Tax Court's filing fee is $60, and it can be waived for taxpayers who can't afford it.

source.title: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund
source.section: Appeals to the Courts: Tax Court

prompt: After a field examination, a taxpayer disagrees with proposed changes of $40,000 for one tax period and wants a conference with Appeals. What must she send?
choices: A petition to the Tax Court
A brief written statement on a small case request form
A formal written protest
Form 12153
answer: A formal written protest
explanation:
After an examination, the IRS usually sends a 30-day letter explaining the proposed changes and the taxpayer's right to appeal. To request an Appeals conference, the taxpayer must file a formal written protest when the total proposed additional tax, penalties and interest for any one tax period is more than $25,000. When it is $25,000 or less, a small case request is enough.

The formal protest must include the taxpayer's name, address and phone number; a statement that they want to appeal; a copy of the letter showing the proposed changes; the periods involved; the items they disagree with and why; the facts and law supporting their position; and a declaration under penalties of perjury. If a representative prepares it, the representative declares whether they know the facts are true.

Exam tip: field examinations always require a written protest. Even below $25,000, a small case request must be in writing for a field audit.

source.title: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree

prompt: During an examination interview, a taxpayer says he wants to consult a representative before answering more questions. What must the IRS generally do?
choices: Finish the interview, because he chose to attend without a representative
End the examination and issue a notice of deficiency
Require him to sign a waiver of his right to representation
Suspend the interview so he can consult a representative
answer: Suspend the interview so he can consult a representative
explanation:
The right to retain representation is one of the ten rights in the Taxpayer Bill of Rights and is explained in Publication 1. During an interview, if the taxpayer clearly asks to consult a representative, the IRS must stop the interview and reschedule it so the taxpayer can do so. The exception is an interview held because of an administrative summons.

A taxpayer can also send an authorized representative (under Form 2848) to the interview instead of attending. The IRS can only require the taxpayer to attend in person if it issues a summons. The taxpayer may record the interview with advance notice, and the IRS can also record it.

Exam tip: if a representative is unreasonably delaying an examination, the IRS can bypass them and contact the taxpayer directly, with a supervisor's approval.

source.title: Publication 1, Your Rights as a Taxpayer

prompt: Under Circular 230, a practitioner may not advise a client to take a position on a return when the position:
choices: Lacks a reasonable basis
Has substantial authority but is not disclosed on the return
Differs from a position taken in a prior year
Has less than a 90% chance of being sustained
answer: Lacks a reasonable basis
explanation:
Circular 230 section 10.34 says a practitioner may not willfully, recklessly or through gross incompetence sign a return or advise a client to take a position on a return that lacks a reasonable basis, is an unreasonable position under section 6694(a), or is a willful attempt to understate tax.

In practice: a position with substantial authority can be taken without disclosure. A position with only a reasonable basis (a relatively low standard, but more than merely arguable) must be adequately disclosed, usually on Form 8275. Positions on tax shelters and reportable transactions need a reasonable belief that they are more likely than not to be sustained. The practitioner must also inform the client of any penalties that are reasonably likely to apply and how disclosure can avoid them.

Exam tip: in order from lowest to highest, the standards are reasonable basis (about 20%), substantial authority (about 40%), and more likely than not (over 50%).

source.title: Treasury Department Circular No. 230, Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service
source.section: §10.34 Standards with respect to tax returns and documents

prompt: A taxpayer files her return three months late with no extension, and pays the $10,000 balance due with it. No minimum penalty or relief applies. What is the combined penalty for filing and paying late?
explanation:
The failure-to-file penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month the return is late, up to 25%. The failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, also up to 25%. For any month when both apply, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty, so the combined rate is 5% a month.

For three months on $10,000: the failure-to-file penalty is 4.5% × 3 = 13.5%, or $1,350, and the failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% × 3 = 1.5%, or $150. The total is $1,500, plus interest. If the return were more than 60 days late, a minimum failure-to-file penalty would apply ($510 for returns due in 2025, or 100% of the tax due if less). The question says no minimum applies.

Exam tip: first-time abatement can remove these penalties for a taxpayer with a clean compliance history for the past three years, even without reasonable cause.

source.title: Failure to file penalty

prompt: For an individual, an understatement of income tax is "substantial" for the 20% accuracy-related penalty when it is more than:
choices: The lesser of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000
$10,000, whatever the size of the correct tax
25% of the gross income shown on the return
The greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000
answer: The greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000
explanation:
The accuracy-related penalty under section 6662 is 20% of the part of an underpayment caused by negligence or disregard of the rules, a substantial understatement of income tax, a substantial valuation misstatement, and certain other causes. For gross valuation misstatements and undisclosed transactions lacking economic substance, the rate is 40%.

For an individual, an understatement is substantial if it is more than the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000. Example: if the correct tax is $80,000 and the understatement is $7,000, the threshold is the greater of $8,000 or $5,000, which is $8,000, so the understatement isn't substantial. The understatement is reduced by items with substantial authority, and by adequately disclosed items with a reasonable basis.

Exam tip: the penalty doesn't apply to any part of an underpayment where the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and good faith.

source.title: Accuracy-related penalty

prompt: What is the civil penalty when part of an underpayment of tax is due to fraud?
choices: 20% of the whole underpayment
75% of the part of the underpayment due to fraud
50% of the part of the underpayment due to fraud
100% of the tax shown on the return
answer: 75% of the part of the underpayment due to fraud
explanation:
Section 6663 imposes a civil fraud penalty of 75% of the part of an underpayment that is due to fraud. Fraud means intentional wrongdoing to evade a tax believed to be owed, such as hiding income, keeping two sets of books or making false entries.

The IRS must prove fraud by clear and convincing evidence. Once it shows that any part of the underpayment is due to fraud, the entire underpayment is treated as fraudulent unless the taxpayer proves which parts aren't. The 20% accuracy-related penalty doesn't apply to the part of the underpayment the fraud penalty covers. A fraudulent return also has no statute of limitations on assessment.

Exam tip: on a joint return, the fraud penalty applies to a spouse only if part of the underpayment is due to that spouse's own fraud.

source.title: Publication 17, Your Federal Income Tax (2025)

prompt: A corporation's president decided to pay suppliers instead of depositing withheld payroll taxes. What is the amount of the trust fund recovery penalty that can be assessed against her personally?
choices: $5,000 for each quarter
20% of the unpaid trust fund taxes
100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes
50% of all unpaid employment taxes, including the employer's share
answer: 100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes
explanation:
Trust fund taxes are amounts an employer withholds from employees and holds in trust for the government: federal income tax withholding and the employees' share of Social Security and Medicare taxes. Under section 6672, any responsible person who willfully fails to collect, account for or pay over these taxes can be held personally liable for a penalty equal to 100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes.

A responsible person has the duty and power to decide which bills get paid, such as an officer, owner or employee who signs checks. Willfully means knowing the taxes were due and choosing to pay other creditors instead. The president knew and chose to pay suppliers, so both tests are met. The employer's share of FICA and FUTA isn't part of the penalty.

Exam tip: before assessing the penalty, the IRS usually interviews potentially responsible people on Form 4180 and sends Letter 1153, which gives 60 days to appeal.

source.title: Employment taxes and the trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP)

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a basis on which the IRS can accept an offer in compromise?
choices: Doubt as to the taxpayer's willingness to pay
Doubt as to collectibility
Effective tax administration
Doubt as to liability
answer: Doubt as to the taxpayer's willingness to pay
explanation:
An offer in compromise is an agreement to settle a tax debt for less than the full amount owed. The IRS can accept an offer on three grounds. Doubt as to liability applies when there is a genuine dispute about whether the tax is owed. Doubt as to collectibility applies when the taxpayer's assets and future income are less than the amount owed. Effective tax administration applies when full collection is possible but would create economic hardship or be unfair and inequitable.

For doubt as to collectibility, the IRS generally expects an offer at least equal to the taxpayer's reasonable collection potential: the net equity in their assets plus their future disposable income. Offers are filed on Form 656 with Form 433-A (OIC) or 433-B (OIC), an application fee, and an initial payment (20% of a lump-sum offer, or the first monthly payment), unless low-income certification applies. Doubt as to liability offers use Form 656-L and need no fee.

Exam tip: while an offer is pending, the collection statute is suspended and the IRS generally can't levy.

source.title: Offer in compromise

prompt: A taxpayer receives a Final Notice of Intent to Levy and Notice of Your Right to a Hearing. What must he do to get a collection due process hearing?
choices: Petition the Tax Court within 90 days of the date of the notice
File Form 9423 within 2 business days of a conference with the collection manager
Pay the tax and then file a claim for refund
File Form 12153 within 30 days of the date of the notice
answer: File Form 12153 within 30 days of the date of the notice
explanation:
A taxpayer is entitled to a collection due process (CDP) hearing with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals after receiving a Notice of Federal Tax Lien filing or a final notice of intent to levy. The request is made on Form 12153, and it must be filed within 30 days of the notice (for a levy notice) or by the date stated in the notice (for a lien notice).

A timely request generally stops levy action for the periods covered, and suspends the collection statute while the hearing is pending. At the hearing, the taxpayer can raise collection alternatives, such as an installment agreement or offer in compromise, spousal defenses, and, in some cases, whether the tax is actually owed. Appeals issues a determination, which the taxpayer can challenge in Tax Court within 30 days.

Exam tip: a request made within one year of the notice gets an equivalent hearing, but it doesn't stop collection and its decision can't be taken to Tax Court.

source.title: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights

prompt: An individual who has filed and paid on time for the past five years now owes $8,000 of income tax and can pay it within three years. What is true of his request for an installment agreement?
choices: The IRS must accept it
The IRS can accept it only with a 20% down payment
The IRS can accept it only after he files a full financial statement
The IRS can accept it only if a federal tax lien is filed first
answer: The IRS must accept it
explanation:
Under section 6159(c), the IRS must accept an individual's installment agreement request (a guaranteed installment agreement) when the tax owed, not counting interest and penalties, is $10,000 or less; the taxpayer has filed all returns and paid all tax for the previous five years and hasn't had an installment agreement during that time; the taxpayer agrees to pay the full amount within three years; and the taxpayer agrees to comply with the tax laws while the agreement is in effect.

This taxpayer owes $8,000, has a clean five-year history and can pay within three years, so the IRS must accept. Taxpayers who owe more can still use a streamlined agreement, generally for balances up to $50,000 paid within 72 months, again without a full financial statement. Requests are made online or on Form 9465. Penalties and interest keep accruing, but the failure-to-pay penalty drops to 0.25% a month while an agreement is in effect (for a timely filed return).

Exam tip: an installment agreement is generally the first collection alternative to suggest before an offer in compromise.

prompt: By when must a taxpayer generally file Form 8857 to request innocent spouse relief from an understatement of tax on a joint return?
choices: Within three years after the joint return was filed
Within two years after the IRS first begins collection activity against that taxpayer
Before the divorce becomes final
Within 90 days after the notice of deficiency
answer: Within two years after the IRS first begins collection activity against that taxpayer
explanation:
There are three kinds of relief from joint liability. Innocent spouse relief (section 6015(b)) is for an understatement caused by the other spouse's erroneous items when the requesting spouse didn't know and had no reason to know of it. Separation of liability relief (section 6015(c)) divides the understatement between spouses who are divorced, legally separated, widowed or haven't lived together for 12 months. Equitable relief (section 6015(f)) covers cases that don't qualify for the others, including tax that was reported but not paid.

Requests for innocent spouse and separation of liability relief must be filed no later than two years after the IRS first began collection activity against the requesting spouse, such as a levy or offset. Equitable relief requests can be filed within the time the IRS has to collect the tax, or for a refund, within the refund claim period.

Exam tip: the IRS must notify the other spouse and let them take part. Domestic abuse is taken into account for the knowledge test.

prompt: What is the difference between a federal tax lien and a levy?
choices: A lien applies to real estate only, and a levy applies to personal property only
A lien is a legal claim against the taxpayer's property that secures the debt, and a levy actually takes the property
There is no difference between the two
A lien takes wages, and a levy takes bank accounts
answer: A lien is a legal claim against the taxpayer's property that secures the debt, and a levy actually takes the property
explanation:
A federal tax lien arises automatically when the IRS assesses a tax, sends a notice and demand for payment, and the taxpayer doesn't pay in full. It is the government's legal claim against all of the taxpayer's current and future property. The IRS may file a public Notice of Federal Tax Lien to alert creditors, which can affect the taxpayer's ability to get credit or sell property.

A levy is the legal seizure of property to satisfy the debt. The IRS can levy wages, bank accounts, Social Security benefits, accounts receivable, vehicles and other property. Before most levies, the IRS must send a final notice of intent to levy and notice of the right to a hearing at least 30 days ahead.

Exam tip: remedies for liens include release (after payment), discharge of specific property, subordination (to let another creditor go first) and withdrawal of the public notice.

prompt: Who must have a preparer tax identification number (PTIN)?
choices: Only preparers who file more than 10 returns a year
Only attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents
Anyone who prepares a return, including unpaid volunteers
Anyone who prepares, or helps prepare, all or substantially all of a federal tax return for compensation
answer: Anyone who prepares, or helps prepare, all or substantially all of a federal tax return for compensation
explanation:
Anyone who, for compensation, prepares or helps prepare all or substantially all of any federal tax return or claim for refund must have a valid PTIN and enter it on the returns they sign. This includes attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents as well as unenrolled preparers.

PTINs are obtained and renewed online every year. Each PTIN expires on December 31, and renewal for the next year opens in mid-October. Supervised employees of attorneys, CPAs or enrolled agents who help prepare returns also need a PTIN, even though they don't sign the return.

Exam tip: paid preparers who fail to put their PTIN on a return they sign can be charged a penalty under section 6695(c) for each failure.

prompt: Form 8867, the paid preparer's due diligence checklist, is NOT required for a return that claims which of the following?
choices: The American opportunity tax credit
The premium tax credit
Head of household filing status
The earned income credit
answer: The premium tax credit
explanation:
Under section 6695(g), a paid preparer who prepares a return claiming the earned income credit, the child tax credit, additional child tax credit or credit for other dependents, the American opportunity tax credit, or head of household filing status must meet four due diligence requirements.

The four requirements are: complete and submit Form 8867 with the return; figure the credits correctly and keep the computation worksheets; meet the knowledge requirement by asking the client questions, documenting the answers and not ignoring information that seems incorrect or incomplete; and keep records for three years. Each failure carries a separate inflation-adjusted penalty for each credit or status claimed on the return.

Exam tip: the premium tax credit is reconciled on Form 8962, but it isn't one of the benefits covered by preparer due diligence.

prompt: For how long must a paid preparer keep a copy of each return prepared, or a list of the taxpayers' names and identification numbers?
choices: Indefinitely
Three years after the close of the return period
One year after the return is filed
Six years after the return is filed
answer: Three years after the close of the return period
explanation:
Under section 6107(b), a signing tax return preparer must keep either a completed copy of each return or claim for refund they prepared, or a list of the taxpayers' names and identification numbers and the tax years, for three years after the close of the return period. The preparer must make it available to the IRS on request. The return period is generally the 12-month period beginning July 1 of each year.

The preparer must also give the taxpayer a completed copy of the return no later than when the return is presented for signature. A penalty under section 6695 applies for each failure to give the taxpayer a copy, or to keep the copy or list, unless the failure is due to reasonable cause.

Exam tip: separate three-year retention rules apply to Form 8867 due diligence records and to Form 8879 e-file signature forms.

prompt: A tax return preparer must generally e-file the individual, estate and trust income tax returns he prepares when he reasonably expects to file how many in a calendar year?
choices: 5 or more
11 or more
50 or more
250 or more
answer: 11 or more
explanation:
Under section 6011(e)(3), a specified tax return preparer must file covered returns electronically. A specified tax return preparer is one who reasonably expects to file 11 or more individual income tax returns (Forms 1040 and 1040-SR) and trust and estate returns (Form 1041) during the calendar year. Members of a firm count the firm's returns together.

A client can choose to file on paper. The preparer must then get a signed and dated statement from the client, keep it, and attach Form 8948 to the paper return explaining why it isn't being e-filed. Hardship waivers can be requested on Form 8944.

Exam tip: the 11-return threshold is separate from the rule for businesses, which must e-file information returns such as Forms W-2 and 1099 if they file 10 or more in total.

prompt: What does an electronic return originator (ERO) do with a signed Form 8879?
choices: Attaches it to the electronic return as a PDF
Destroys it once the return is accepted
Mails it to the IRS within three business days
Keeps it for three years from the return due date or the date the IRS received the return, whichever is later
answer: Keeps it for three years from the return due date or the date the IRS received the return, whichever is later
explanation:
Form 8879, the IRS e-file Signature Authorization, lets the taxpayer authorize the ERO to enter or create their self-selected PIN, or to use the Practitioner PIN method, to sign the electronic return. The taxpayer signs Form 8879 after reviewing the return and before it is transmitted.

The ERO keeps the completed Form 8879 for three years from the return's due date or the date the IRS received it, whichever is later. It can be kept on paper or electronically, and it is provided to the IRS only on request. The ERO must not transmit the return before receiving the signed Form 8879.

Exam tip: if the return is changed after the taxpayer signs, and the amounts differ by more than $50 in total income or AGI or $14 in total tax, federal withholding, refund or amount owed, the taxpayer must sign a new Form 8879.

prompt: A preparer knowingly sells a client list, with income details taken from the returns, to an insurance agent without the clients' consent. What criminal penalty applies under section 7216?
choices: A $50 penalty for each disclosure, with no possibility of prison
None, because only civil penalties apply to preparers
A misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $1,000, up to one year in prison, or both
A felony, with a fine of up to $100,000 and up to five years in prison
answer: A misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $1,000, up to one year in prison, or both
explanation:
Section 7216 makes it a crime for a tax return preparer to knowingly or recklessly disclose or use tax return information for any purpose other than preparing the return, unless the regulations allow it or the taxpayer consents. Selling client information to an insurance agent without consent is a clear violation.

The crime is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, up to one year in prison, or both, plus the costs of prosecution. When the disclosure is connected with an identity theft crime, the fine can be up to $100,000. Section 6713 adds a civil penalty of $250 for each unauthorized disclosure or use, up to $10,000 a year. Consent must be in writing, signed by the taxpayer, and meet the format rules of Rev. Proc. 2013-14.

Exam tip: a preparer may use client information to offer the preparer's own tax-related services without consent, but needs consent to offer other products, such as insurance or investments.

prompt: What must every professional tax preparer have in place under the Federal Trade Commission's Safeguards Rule?
choices: A written information security plan
A cyber liability insurance policy
A bonded off-site storage provider
An annual security audit by the IRS
answer: A written information security plan
explanation:
Tax preparers are financial institutions under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, so they must follow the FTC Safeguards Rule. The rule requires a written information security plan (WISP) to protect client data, sized for the firm and the sensitivity of its data.

The plan must name a qualified person to oversee it, assess risks, put safeguards in place (such as encryption, multi-factor authentication and access controls), train staff, monitor and test the safeguards, oversee service providers, have an incident response plan, and be updated regularly. Publication 4557 and Publication 5708 give the IRS's guidance and a sample plan.

Exam tip: preparers renewing their PTIN confirm that they know about their data security obligations, and e-file providers must report data thefts to the IRS promptly.
